Project picker.what: A projects panel on the left, collapsible to a rail and resizable, for opening a bundled sample project into the editor (the sample catalog is empty today).

Repo load from GitHub.what: Type owner/repo, or open an env/<owner>/<repo> address, and that GitHub repo is cloned into the workspace, history and all, and the address bar shows it.

Sign-in and account.what: An optional sign-in (GitHub or email) for private repos and commits, with your account, where you're signed in, signing out everywhere and deleting the account.

Commit to GitHub.what: Push the whole workspace back to the repo and branch it was loaded from, with a commit message, from the top bar.

Playground links.what: Open a TypeScript Playground link here as a real workspace (swap its host for the editor's), and share your workspace as a link the Playground opens too.

Docking editors into windows.what: Move a VS Code editor into its own window docked around the editor, and show a docked window (such as a preview) as an editor tab.

Theme follows your system.what: The editor switches light or dark with the operating system, and the surrounding chrome takes on VS Code's colours.

Pane beside every editor.what: A strip of tabbed views beside the code (the Margin and each extension's), level with the lines they describe, or shown instead as VS Code's own code lenses, hints and hovers.

Rule editor.what: One editor for every rule about what a program may do (allow, deny, give a value), opened under the Rules tree from a stop, the Margin or a preview prompt.

File and text search.what: Quick Open, Find in Files and extensions' file searches over the workspace, honouring files-to-include and files-to-exclude globs.

Packages and types from the CDN.what: Any import type-checks and go-to-definition reaches real package source without installing anything, at dependency versions pinned for everyone.

Annotations that stay on their code.what: Notes, rules and evidence placed on a piece of code, by the editor or an extension, stay on that code through edits, moves and reformatting.

Run from the shell.what: A Run menu in the top bar runs the file in the editor in the debugger, or one of the workspace's scripts and tasks, showing a running service's preview instead of starting it twice.

The workspace terminal.what: A bash-like terminal on the workspace's files with npm, node, git, vite and other commands, which VS Code tasks also run in.

Run a file in the debugger.what: Run (the editor's play button) runs the open file in the debugger, the one way every program runs, whichever debugger is set to run it.

Terminal node runs in the debugger.what: Typing `node <file>` in the terminal starts a debug session that prints and reads input in that terminal, and Ctrl-C stops it.

Stepping debugger with step back.what: Breakpoints, stepping forward and backward, and variables, on a predictable clock whose timer waits can be skipped or made real.

Explore orderings.what: Runs a program under every ordering of its events and shows the different outcomes, so bugs that depend on order turn up.

Tests run in the debugger.what: `node --test` runs test files in the debugger with breakpoints and stepping, and remembers which code each test reached.

Preview's dev server as a debug session.what: A running preview's dev server shows up in Run and Debug with a Stop button, and its output goes to the Debug Console.

Breakpoints in a page's code.what: A breakpoint in a web app's page code records what was in scope each time its line ran and shows it in the margin, and a recorded call can be stepped through again in the debugger.
Breakpoints in a page's code.docs: packages/editor/RUNNING.md, *Apps: recorded stops, not live ones*

Debug toolbar in the preview title bar.what: The pause, step, restart and stop buttons also appear in the preview window's title bar and control the same session.

Package scripts as tasks and the run pic.what: Every package.json script is a task you can run, listed in Run Task and in the shell's run picker, and each runs in its own terminal.

Agents drive the debugger.what: An AI agent can start, step, pace and stop debug sessions, send them input, set values in them, answer a call's question, set breakpoints, explore orderings, and read what the margin and the Rules view show.

Programs, services and what's running.what: A program started from the terminal, a task or Run runs in the debugger with its output streamed back, and a server it starts opens a preview; a status bar entry lists what's running, stops each, and says how each ended.

Live values in the margin.what: Beside the code, each line shows the values it produced when it ran, one column per turn of a loop; you can hold a column or pick a call to look at, and while stopped the latest value appears inline.

Past runs, as balls.what: Each run of a file is kept on this machine, and picking it at the top of the margin shows its values and how it ended.

Live runs after an edit.what: The file you're editing runs again on save and on a timer so the margin stays current, without asking you anything, and a call these unwatched runs can't make can be pinned to a value it returned before or given a rule.

Mock a value.what: Give the program different command-line arguments, or a variable a different value, either once at a stop or on every run by a rule.
Mock a value.docs: packages/editor/RUNTIME-EVIDENCE.md, *Mocking a value — and one way to run*

Coverage in the gutter.what: After a run, marks beside each line show whether it ran and how often, and the same colors appear in the scrollbar.

Preview windows.what: Running a dev server opens movable windows onto your app, as many per server as you like, hot-reloading on every change and showing your app's console and errors in the editor.
Preview windows.docs: packages/editor/ARCHITECTURE.md, *The live preview, end to end*

In-browser dev server.what: Your app's dev server (Vite) runs inside the browser on the workspace's files, and a program's own server is served to the preview the same way; an agent can force its cold-start race to check for transform errors.
In-browser dev server.docs: packages/editor/ARCHITECTURE.md, *The live preview, end to end*

Capability prompts for previews.what: When your app reaches the network, a WebSocket or WebRTC that the policy hasn't decided, its preview window asks you; a preview nobody is watching is answered from what the call returned last time.

Preview DevTools.what: Chrome's DevTools docked under a preview window (console, elements, network), and the same DevTools protocol for agents.

Preview CPU profiles.what: Profile a preview's page on demand, and automatically when it keeps running slow, saving each profile as a .cpuprofile mapped back to the lines you wrote.

Answer a call where it stops.what: When a run reaches a call that touches files, the network or commands and nothing has decided it yet, the run stops on that line and asks in the margin: allow, skip or deny, for this call, this run or always, or make a rule.

Real effects, decided per call.what: Your policy decides whether each file, network or command call a run or preview makes really happens; what an allowed call returned is recorded so a rule can give it back later, and what each run did is kept.

Capability findings in the code.what: Calls that reach the network, files, commands, the environment or eval are underlined in the code and listed in Problems, with the actual URL or path filled in by a background run.

Capability calls panel.what: A panel lists the program's capability calls and lets you allow, deny or clear each one; a denied call is marked as an error in the code.

Dependency baseline and exceptions.what: What each dependency's own code can do is recorded when it's added, and the Exceptions view shows anything that goes beyond that and how each run's calls were answered.

Rules.what: The Rules view lists every rule as a sentence, in the order rules are checked, where you can add, open, edit and remove them.

Rules placed in the code.what: A rule tied to a line stays with its code through edits, shows as a gutter mark with its sentence on hover, and can be re-placed when its place is lost.
Rules placed in the code.docs: packages/editor/RUNNING.md, *A rule placed in the code*

What went through this code, on hover.what: Hovering code shows which values passed through it across runs, how often they were empty, what kinds they were next to the declared type, and how often each branch ran.
What went through this code, on hover.docs: packages/editor/RUNTIME-EVIDENCE.md, *Second slice: values, branches and types*

What could go, in purple.what: Code the runs show was never needed, such as a `?.` that never met an empty value or a branch never taken, is tinted purple with a quick fix to remove it, and the Suggestions view lists them for every file.
What could go, in purple.docs: packages/editor/RUNTIME-EVIDENCE.md, *Fourth slice: what could go, in purple, across inputs*

Performance monitor.what: The status bar and a Monitor view of small live charts show the editor's memory, workspace fill, long frames and errors as they happen.

Runtime evidence kept in git.what: What runs and previews observed (which code ran, the values that passed, whether functions stayed pure) is summed and committed beside the code with each run's envelope and the machine it ran on; you choose how much of a preview is recorded.

ESLint.what: Real ESLint checks your code as you type, with quick fixes, fix-all on save, formatting, and the usual eslint.* settings.

Spell check.what: The real cspell engine spell-checks code and prose.

Type queries.what: A `// ^?` comment under an expression shows that expression's type at the end of the comment, as in the TypeScript Playground.

Unparsable files flagged.what: A file the editor can't parse gets a warning in Problems, because notes and evidence can't attach to it until it parses again.

Review panel.what: A changes panel on the right listing changed files, with a side-by-side diff, per-file discard and a commit box, like GitHub Desktop.

Your edits since the last commit.what: Every edit burst since the last commit is recorded per file and shown as small chunks grouped by the code they touched, surviving reloads.

Git in the browser.what: The workspace is a real git repository, with no git binary, which VS Code's Source Control view and extensions read and commit to.

Push to GitHub.what: A branch of the workspace's git pushed to the GitHub repository it was loaded from, through the editor's sign-in, its commits by the signed-in user; branches made and switched to.

Review by hunk.what: The working tree's changes as hunks with ids, each with BABLR's cosmetic verdict and the features whose code it's in; a commit or a discard takes some of a file's hunks, by an agent's ids or the review panel's line picks.

Source Control for git.what: The Source Control view shows staged and unstaged changes with diffs against the last commit, and commits from its input box.

Formatting-only changes marked.what: Each change is judged formatting-only or meaningful; a file whose changes are only whitespace, semicolons or comments gets a badge and a dimmed name in Source Control and the Explorer.

Notes on code.what: A note attached to a piece of code follows that code as it moves and changes; when the code is gone, the note waits in Problems to be re-placed or dismissed.

What your edits change.what: When you pause typing, the History output says which features your edits added, removed or changed, and whether runs used them.
What your edits change.docs: packages/silo/README.md, *Derived history: features, reach, what runs say*

Feature ledger drift in Problems.what: Where what's been decided about a feature no longer matches the code, a problem says so on the ledger and offers both ways out.
Feature ledger drift in Problems.docs: packages/silo/README.md, *The feature ledger: code keeps its place, or goes*

Dormant features marked in History.what: A way in whose files CI's runs load and whose code they never run is tinted purple where it's registered, with what deleting it frees, and a choice to keep it for 90 days or remove it.
Dormant features marked in History.docs: packages/silo/README.md, *The feature ledger: code keeps its place, or goes*

Features map.what: A side bar of the program as its features, in the Insights monitor's cards: a card per area, a block per feature sized by its code, a legend in their colors; clicking one focuses on it and the rest of the workspace steps back (Explorer dots, open editors dimmed, its name in the status bar); a feature's status is set from the Command Palette.

Agent workspace tools.what: An agent reads, writes, edits, globs and greps the workspace's files, reads what the terminals printed, and checks status, diffs and commits with git: through the editor, not a shell.

A change's problems.what: The TypeScript and ESLint problems a change made and the ones it fixed, against HEAD: its changed files and the files importing them, each checked now and as HEAD had it, with what wasn't checked said.

What a way in reaches.what: For a way in (a command, hub request, tool, core module, setting, view), the feature that owns it, where it's registered, what removing it would free and leave by hand, and everywhere code, tests and docs name it: silo remove's plan, written nowhere.

Tests for agents.what: Which tests a change reaches, by the traces of their runs here (stale when they ran code it has altered, and the test files never run named), and test files run in the debugger with each test's result as data: outcome, error, a failed assertion's sides, time, and how it came out before.

Agent view of the editor.what: An agent reads what's on screen as data: the active file, cursor and open tabs, the Problems view, and the notifications showing.

Agent connection.what: Each open tab offers its tools to an agent through debug-mcp, addressed by tab so one agent can drive several, plus a scripting hook for automation on localhost.

Event Sheet.what: Shows the game the open file belongs to as a map of its objects, rules, behaviors and components, each of which opens its code, and shows this file's part of the game beside the code.

Build a game by painting a level.what: Start a new game, paint a level on a grid with one-click objects, pick systems, and generate the game's code into the project.

Plug an interpreter into Run.what: Another extension's debugger can be the one Run starts; its worker reads and writes the workspace through the editor, under the same policy as any run.

Starter interpreter.what: A template extension you can fork, whose interpreter runs a file when you press Run, and which is rebuilt and reloaded into the editor as you change it.

Starter code renderer.what: The template's Reopen Editor With → Rendered view: a custom editor that shows a file rendered and writes your changes back to its text.

Workbench boot.what: The editor page boots VS Code's workbench in a frame, hands it the workspace, and keeps the two talking even when the editor is popped out.

Workspace filesystem.what: One in-memory workspace shared by the editor, terminal, previews and debugger, saved across reloads, where a change made anywhere is seen everywhere.

Runs on a static host.what: A service worker makes the editor work from a plain static site: it supplies the isolation the editor needs (after one reload), serves package files from a CDN and answers preview requests.

Extensions by URL.what: Load extensions from outside the editor (an interpreter or renderer from editor-contrib) by URL, reloading as they're rebuilt.

Live architecture view and metrics.what: A live diagram of the editor's parts and the messages between them, checked against its rules, and per-second memory, timing and traffic numbers for the monitor.

Sign in with GitHub.what: Signs a person in to the editor or the admin app with their GitHub account, through a GitHub App that reads only their numeric GitHub id.
Sign in with GitHub.docs: packages/api/README.md, *A GitHub App, not an OAuth App*

Sign in by email code.what: Signs a person in with a one-time code emailed to their address, which they type in or reach through the email's link.

Sign in with a password, and reset it.what: Lets a person set a password, sign in with their email and password, and reset a forgotten password using a code sent by email.

Two-factor sign-in.what: Adds a second step to sign-in: a code from an authenticator app or an emailed code, plus recovery codes for getting back in.

Sign in with a passkey.what: Lets a person register passkeys, sign in with one instead of a password, and remove them.

Link sign-in methods and merge accounts.what: Lets a person add a GitHub account or another email address to their account, and merge in a separate account that already had it.

Hosted sign-in and DPoP tokens for clien.what: Gives every client app one locked-down sign-in page on the API (started by a pushed authorization request), so no app's own page ever sees a password; the app then gets short-lived DPoP-bound access tokens and rotating refresh tokens, plus OAuth metadata and a JWKS.

Manage your sign-ins and delete your acc.what: Lets a person see the sessions signed in as them, revoke one or all of them, and delete their account; deleted data is purged after a grace period.
Manage your sign-ins and delete your acc.docs: packages/api/README.md, *Identity and the data we keep*

Your account page.what: One Preact account page, shared by the editor and the admin app, for managing ways to sign in, passkeys, two-factor and a password.

GitHub API proxy.what: Passes the editor's GitHub API calls and a clone's git reads through to GitHub with the user's GitHub token kept on the server, and never allows a push.

Admin: sign-in and roles.what: Gives the admin app its own sign-in, separate from the editor's, and shows each person only the pages their roles allow.

Admin: overview and users.what: Shows an overview page and the list of accounts, and for each user their identities, sessions and audit rows.

Admin: sign-ins and their timelines.what: Lists live sign-ins and lets an admin revoke one or open its timeline: the requests, editor events, audit rows and errors in order.

Admin: architecture.what: Shows the API as it describes itself: its routes, data stores and tables, the GitHub calls it passes through, who calls it, and what it calls.

Rate limits.what: Refuses sign-in, token and error-report requests that go over per-IP or per-target limits, before doing the work.

Unusual sign-ins.what: Scores each sign-in's requests and client against a learned model of normal behavior (without keeping the actual values), and lists the unusual ones, worst first, in the admin app.

Tamper-evident audit log.what: Records every security event (sign-ins, refusals, account changes) in D1 and in locked R2 copies that can't be changed or deleted, and shows the log in the admin app.

Kill switch and switches.what: Lets the owner pause the whole API (maintenance mode) or smaller parts of it from the admin app, and the health and status endpoints report it.
Kill switch and switches.docs: packages/api/README.md, *The kill switch (O1) and narrower switches (O8)*

Traffic and cost guard.what: Shows Cloudflare's traffic analytics (top paths, user agents, status codes) in the admin app, checks the account's spend every hour, and alerts or pauses if usage runs away.

Tripwire.what: Checks every row a signed-in request reads and treats any row that belongs to another user as an incident, alerting the owner.

Errors with quotable ids.what: Every uncaught error, the API's and the editor's alike, gets an id the person is shown to quote; errors are grouped, and the admin app shows each occurrence with a source-mapped stack and, for a signed-in session, what happened just before.

Email, inbox and the Mail page.what: Sends the API's email, receives mail for its own addresses, runs a full email sign-in smoke test, sends alerts to the owner, and shows all of this on the admin app's Mail page.

Redacted logging.what: Sends all of the API's logs and traces through one allowlist, so nothing personal or secret is ever logged.

Sites on unusuallygood.dev.what: Serves the root domain (which redirects browsers to the editor and asks anything else to pay over x402), the editor and the admin app as Cloudflare sites; only the root domain runs a Worker.

debug-mcp server.what: Runs a local collector that the editor's hubs connect to over a WebSocket, and offers what they send to an agent as MCP tools over stdio.

Query logs and spans.what: Lets an agent query the live editor's log records and timed spans from all its contexts, or wait until a matching record arrives.

Metrics.what: Samples gauges in every context once a second (memory, frame rate, long frames, durations, data channels) and lets an agent query them.

Live architecture and payload capture.what: Reports every context (hubs, workers, extension hosts, webviews, network endpoints) and the traffic between them, with optional capture of message payloads, for an agent and for the editor's architecture view.

Connected tabs and hub tree health.what: Finds the editor tabs and preview apps connected right now (flagging ones on an outdated protocol) so tools can target one, and gives a health snapshot of the hub tree.

Page tools.what: Lets a page offer its own tools, such as evaluating JavaScript or running a CSS selector in the live page, which debug-mcp passes to an agent for one tab.

Observe an app (opt-in debug link).what: One call that sends an app's logs, console output and errors onto its hub, keeps a preview app's records under their own scope, and connects to debug-mcp on localhost or when ?debug is set.

Composable message hubs.what: A message bus for each window, frame or worker, linked into a tree with permissions on each link, so a message crosses a boundary only when something on the other side wants it; it comes with a simulated network for deterministic tests.

Hub request/reply.what: Lets one context serve a named request and another context call it across the hub tree, with timeouts and an error when nobody answers.

Hub links over WebRTC, and tab lobbies.what: Links hubs in two pages over a WebRTC data channel, and groups a browser's open tabs into a lobby with one tab chosen as host.

silo features.what: Lists every way into a program (commands, views, settings, buttons, agent tools, hub requests and more) by reading its code.
silo features.docs: packages/silo/README.md, *Derived history: features, reach, what runs say (built 2026-10-12; the feature layer parked)*

silo history.what: Tells what changed in a program from snapshots of its code along git's first-parent history, never from commit messages.
silo history.docs: packages/silo/README.md, *Derived history: features, reach, what runs say (built 2026-10-12; the feature layer parked)*

silo check.what: Reports where the feature ledger or this manifest and the code disagree (a stopped feature still in the code, a removed one still documented, a way in no feature owns) and fails CI on it.
silo check.docs: packages/silo/README.md, *The feature ledger: code keeps its place, or goes (designed 2026-10-12; step 1 built 2026-10-23)*

silo status.what: Records a decision about a feature (active, experimental, stopped and so on) in the shared feature ledger.
silo status.docs: packages/silo/README.md, *The feature ledger: code keeps its place, or goes (designed 2026-10-12; step 1 built 2026-10-23)*

silo remove and restore.what: Takes a feature out of the code (the files only it uses, plus its manifest entries) and leaves a tombstone that can bring it back later.
silo remove and restore.docs: packages/silo/README.md, *The feature ledger: code keeps its place, or goes (designed 2026-10-12; step 1 built 2026-10-23)*

silo coverage.what: Shows what the runs saved in .silo/ executed, commit by commit: what started or stopped running, and what was never reached.
silo coverage.docs: packages/silo/README.md, *Which tests reach what (designed 2026-10-22; the record built 2026-10-23)*

silo init.what: Sets up .silo/ in a repository, with its git settings and a baseline of what the code imports.

silo install.what: Installs dependencies with the project's package manager, skipping anything published in the last week.

Run TypeScript in the interpreter.what: Runs TypeScript source straight from its syntax tree, synchronously or async, and returns the value of the last expression.

tsval step debugger.what: Steps through a run one step at a time, pauses and resumes it, sets breakpoints, and snapshots or forks the running state.

Host seams, modules and types.what: Lets a host inspect every value and call that crosses in from the host, watch statements and coverage, hook async calls, resolve imports (almostnode does this in the editor), and optionally add TypeScript's type checker.

Explore event-loop schedules.what: Runs a program under every distinct event-loop ordering to find all its possible outcomes and races, each with a schedule that replays it.

Conformance suites.what: Tests tsval against test262 and TypeScript's own test cases, with scripts to fetch, sample and report on them.

Parse TypeScript into a lossless CST.what: Our own BABLR grammar for the TypeScript subset tsval runs; it parses source into a syntax tree that keeps every character, as spans (sync or async), and has a command-line parser and a parse version for checking caches.

In-browser Node runtime (almostnode).what: Runs bundled Node programs, such as language servers, on the browser's main thread, with Node's built-in modules, an in-memory file system, and HTTP servers that a service worker routes requests to.
In-browser Node runtime (almostnode).docs: packages/almostnode/README.md, *Node's built-ins: unenv, Node's own code, and ours where we must differ*

Editor API: run contract for debuggers.what: What a debugger extension and its worker send and answer during a run: custom debug events (values, coverage, effects, ended, ask and others), requests (decide, stdin, getCoverage), a live-values recorder, recorded values for replay, the workspace's files as almostnode's VirtualFS, and the editor's network probes.

Editor API: annotations and pane views.what: Lets an extension attach things to a range of code so they stay with that code as the file changes, and add a tab beside every editor drawn from its own data.

Editor API: capability policy and gate.what: Lets an extension read the capability policy and a run's effects, get the gate's verdict, run untrusted code in a locked-down realm, and read or edit rules.

Editor API: what the editor keeps.what: Lets an extension read the runtime evidence kept for a file, CPU profiles, whether something is a service or a task, how a worker failed, and the editor's git status with BABLR's verdict on each change.

Web Awesome lint rules.what: ESLint rules that flag native HTML elements that have a Web Awesome equivalent, and HTML or CSS written inside strings.

Brand theme.what: Sets up Web Awesome with its design tokens adjusted for the brand, following the system's light or dark mode, with or without Web Awesome's native styles, and kept within a size budget.

Theme follows VS Code's color theme.what: Maps the theme onto whichever VS Code color theme is active in the workbench.

Web Awesome components through the theme.what: The only way for app code to load the Web Awesome components it is allowed to use.

Recipes, surface styles and Stitches.what: Gives each part of the app its own styles and the app's shared shapes as recipe classes, all written with Stitches in an ordered set of style layers.

Published theme components.what: Components published for use outside the app: the movable, collapsible <app-window> element (and an appWindow() function), plus caption, code, frame and toolbar recipes, each a class you get from a function call.

VS Code look for Web Awesome.what: A published Web Awesome theme in VS Code's default colors that follows the live color theme when used inside VS Code or a webview.
VS Code look for Web Awesome.docs: packages/theme/README.md, *The look: Web Awesome as VS Code*

Release pipeline.what: Each push to main tests, builds and publishes every package as a GitHub release tarball and deploys the site, with no npm registry.

Architecture suites and performance budg.what: Browser suites tour the real editor (runs, previews, capabilities, sessions), record what each test reached for CI's evidence, and hold boot time, hover latency, a large repo's load and memory to budgets.

Weekly ledger cleanup.what: Each week CI runs `silo check` and opens one pull request deleting the first dormant way in that `silo remove` can take out.
